The default size limit for individual file uploads (max_file_size) is 10MiB and the maximum total request size allowed for a single multipart upload request defaults to 50MiB (dsid_ae068ee4aa9640159427cd941bef0238.md).

* The implementation enforces a configurable limit for max_file_size with a default of 10MiB (dsid_ae068ee4aa9640159427cd941bef0238.md).
* When a part exceeds the max_file_size, the system returns a 413 error with a JSON body specifying the limit in bytes as 10485760 (dsid_ae068ee4aa9640159427cd941bef0238.md).
* The system enforces configurable limits, including max_total_request_size which defaults to 50MiB (dsid_ae068ee4aa9640159427cd941bef0238.md).
* These defaults are conservative and can be overridden at the tenant or route level via API config (dsid_ae068ee4aa9640159427cd941bef0238.md).
* The limits for max_file_size (default 10MiB), max_total_request_size (default 50MiB), and max_parts_count (default 20) are configurable and can be overridden at the tenant or route level via API config (dsid_ae068ee4aa9640159427cd941bef0238.md).
* Users who require larger file uploads can update their tenant config or use Redwood Dedicated with higher quotas (dsid_ae068ee4aa9640159427cd941bef0238.md).
* The system enforces explicit size checks for specific whitelisted Content-Type values, which include text/*, image/*, application/json, and application/octet-stream (dsid_ae068ee4aa9640159427cd941bef0238.md).

context_chunks.text: Motivation: users integrating tool/function calling and file uploads via the OpenAI-compatibility endpoints were sending a wide variety of content-types and very large multipart requests which caused inconsistent runtime behavior, high memory pressure, and unexpected acceptance of unsupported payloads. This PR introduces a focused, backwards-compatible implementation for multipart/form-data parsing on the OpenAI-compatibility path, strict Content-Type validation for tool/file inputs, and deterministic payload limits both per-file and per-request. Summary of changes: 1) Add a streaming-safe multipart parser that yields parts rather than buffering entire requests; 2) Validate Content-Type of each part (whitelist: text/*, image/*, application/json, application/octet-stream with explicit size checks); 3) Enforce configurable limits: max_file_size (default 10MiB), max_total_request_size (default 50MiB), max_parts_count (default 20). These defaults are conservative and documented; they can be overridden at tenant or route level via API config. 4) Hook validation into the OpenAI-compat layer so existing client integrations get predictable errors (400/413) with structured error bodies when inputs are rejected. 5) Add detailed unit and integration tests and end-to-end tests for streaming uploads and for the dedicated Dedicated/Private ingress paths. Backwards compatibility notes: this does not change the non-multipart JSON body semantics. Existing users who relied on accepting arbitrary large file uploads should update their tenant config or use Redwood Dedicated with higher quotas. Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind feature.enable_multipart_input (off by default); staged rollout to internal dogfood tenants, then gradual roll to 10%, 50%, 100% via config rollout.

Motivation: Close a set of subtle incompatibilities between our /v1/chat.completions adapter and OpenAI's behavior that have been causing developer friction in streaming function-call flows and stop/logprobs handling. This PR implements a compact 'parameter normalizer' layer and a streaming framing/backpressure handshake to make the adapter tolerant of real-world clients and OpenAI-style payloads. Summary of changes: - Parameter normalizer: unify and sanitize incoming params (max_tokens, temperature, top_p, n, presence_penalty) and map them to our internal API consistently; accept both string and numeric encodings, preserve explicit nulls, and prefer client-provided values for edge cases. - Role aliasing: accept and normalize role names coming from clients ("assistant", "system", "user", "tool", and legacy aliases like "ai" or "bot"); ensure role is preserved in both final and streaming envelopes. - Stop sequence deduplication: support stop as string or array; expand single-string stops into an array; dedupe overlapping sequences (e.g. ["

", "


"]) and maintain order stability to match OpenAI semantics. - Sparse logprobs: add an opt-in sparse_logprobs mode that mirrors OpenAI's sparse token-level logprob structure when requested; keep heavy-weight computation behind an explicit flag to avoid perf regressions. - Streaming framing & backpressure: introduce a light handshake in the stream start (sent as first SSE/delta) that communicates our token framing and heartbeat expectations; implement backpressure signaling for HTTP/2 clients to avoid partial JSON objects when a client pauses mid-stream. - Function-call streaming support: improve chunking for function_call.name/arguments so that streaming deltas assemble deterministically into valid JSON payloads even across reconnects; final chunk action inserts a stable end-of-function marker to make reconstruction robust.

Motivation: Customers using the OpenAI Responses family expect stable streaming semantics, reliable tool/function call signal delivery, and preservation of determinism hints (seed/RNG) and user metadata when we bridge from our internal Responses v9-compatible runtime to the OpenAI API shape. This PR adds a resilience layer that: 1) performs backpressure-aware chunking and reassembly for streaming frames to avoid partial json/toolcall corruption on slow clients, 2) proxies a lightweight 'tool-signal' envelope so function/tool-calling boundaries are deterministic across retries and reconnections, and 3) forwards seed/determinism flags and a subset of user metadata transparently through the compatibility layer. What this changes (summary): consistent chunk framing and reassembly on the server and client-facing bridge; explicit tool-signal envelope that annotates tool-call start/end + unique tool invocation id; passthrough of 'rng_seed' and 'deterministic' attributes from our Responses request model into the OpenAI-compatible response attributes; metadata routing (user-provided tags/trace id) added to response attributes and to audit logs so downstream services (console, evals) see the same identifiers. Compatibility notes: We keep the OpenAI-compatible surface stable for existing callers. Default behavior is identical unless callers set determinism/seed or rely on streaming reconnects; in those cases the bridge guarantees idempotent framing (replay-safe chunk markers) and consistent toolcall reassembly. There are small opt-ins: the 'tool-signal' envelope is only applied when callers include a 'enable_tool_signal' flag (default true for our hosted API). For private deployments customers can opt-out via config.

**Customer content (MUST remain within pinned region(s))**
- Prompt / messages / input text (including system prompts provided by customer)
- Tool/function call arguments provided by customer
- Uploaded documents or retrieved passages (RAG payloads) provided by customer
- Model outputs (including partial streaming tokens)
- Embeddings input text and embeddings vectors derived from customer text
- Rerank inputs (candidate passages) and rerank outputs derived from those passages
- Fine-tuning / adapter payloads if routed through Hosted API pathways (not in scope for v1 feature, but classification applies)
- Any debug payloads that include raw request/response bodies
- Any derived artifacts that can reconstruct content (e.g., token logs, decoded segments, sampled prompt fragments)

**Not customer content (may be processed outside pinned region(s) under constraints below)**
- Non-content operational metadata that does not include request/response bodies and cannot reasonably be used to reconstruct them (see “Allowed cross-region metadata”). Notes:
- Whether content includes PII is not determinative; **all prompts/outputs are treated as sensitive content**. - “Derived” includes transformations (tokenization, embedding vectors, compression) if they are computed from customer text/output. ### 2) Enforcement boundary: “Where residency applies”
For pinned orgs/projects/API keys, **all handling of customer content** must remain in allowed region(s) for:
- **Request routing** and execution (including retries and fallbacks)
- **Background work** that uses the request payload or output (e.g., async logging of bodies, eval capture, replay queues)
- **Persistence and caching** of any form of request/response content
- **Observability signals** that contain content (logs/traces/debug captures)

Residency enforcement is evaluated at request time by the gateway/routing policy engine and must be **deterministic** (same policy + same request context → same allow/block outcome).

Issue summary:
Customer reports sustained 429 responses across a set of sliced ingest workers after migrating ingestion to a Dedicated pool. The traffic mix is: low-latency chat calls (priority=high) and large multi-part embedding uploads (priority=background). After the migration, background uploads are intermittently exhausting burst credits at the per-route layer and causing opaque 429s for high-priority short calls during peak windows. Impact:
- ~30% of short chat requests returned 429 between 09:00-11:30 PDT on 2026-03-10 for Streamly AI. - Customer reports user-facing errors and retry amplification in their orchestrator. - Business impact: partial degradation of their real-time features during peak ingest windows. Environment:
- Dedicated pool: dp-132-usw
- Region: us-west
- Ingest coordinator version: 2026.02.3
- Rate-limiter service version: 1.14.0-canary Observed behaviour:
- Persistent 429s reported by customer for short-lived chat requests coincident with high concurrency uploads. - Throttle headers (when present) show per-route-window exhaustion; some requests show no X-RateLimit headers (opaque 429). Expected behaviour:
- High-priority interactive calls should be isolated into a small burst pool and not experience 429s while background uploads borrow burst credit from a separate pool (or be rate-limited gracefully). Customer asks:
- Why are small chat calls getting 429s when their load is relatively small? - How to configure priority classes and burst pools for dedicated pools to prevent this? 1) Use the customer's traffic shape: 100 concurrent short chat requests (avg 50ms) + 20 parallel multipart embedding uploads (avg 45s each). 2) Route both traffic shapes through the dedicated pool dp-132-usw with current priority-class config (default: interactive=high, background=low). 3) Start background uploads in a tight window to simulate a scheduled flush (cron at 09:00). 4) Observe 429s on interactive calls between 09:00-09:30 when background uploads ramp up.

If unresolved after SLA window (4 hours), escalate to Tier 3.

It is intended to: align SRE, Product, and Customer Success during SLO degradations; minimize time-to-customer-remediation; and create consistent inputs for post-incident reviews and error-budget decisions.

Audience
- On-call SREs
- SRE leads and managers
- Incident commanders (ICs)

Principles
1) Tie every SLO alert to an explicit customer-impact tier (1–4).
2) Automate low-friction routing and remediation for common degradations.
3) Escalate proactively for any Tier 1/2 customer impact.
4) Preserve evidence for postmortems and error-budget reconciliations.

Definitions
- SLO: Service Level Objective (e.g., request_latency_p95 <= 200ms).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO target over the defined rolling window.
- Customer-impact tier: a 1–4 classification used to route and prioritize incident response.

Customer-impact tiers (quick guide)
| Tier | User-visible symptoms | Business effect | Escalation urgency | Owner to notify |
|------|----------------------|-----------------|-------------------|----------------|
| 1 | Widespread request failures or complete service outage across regions | Severe revenue/customer retention impact | Immediate (page) | SRE lead + Product PM + CS Director |
| 2 | Large subset of customers impacted (major tenants) or major feature down | Significant business disruption for key customers | High (page + slack) | SRE oncall + Product owner + CS manager |
| 3 | Localized errors, degraded latency for non-critical endpoints | Minor customer annoyance, limited support tickets | Medium (slack alert) | On-call SRE + Feature owner |
| 4 | Minor latency increase or transient errors with no customer tickets | No immediate business impact | Low (ticket) | On-call SRE |

Classification algorithm (operational)
1) Alert receives telemetry: detector alerts on SLI breach or error-budget burn (alerting config).
2) Metrics enrichment: pull impact signals (affected tenant count, region distribution, top N tenants by RPS, open support tickets matching pattern).
3) Heuristics engine evaluates the following scores (0–100): failure-scope, severity, customer-exposure.
4) Combined score maps to Tier: Score >= 80 -> Tier 1; 60–79 -> Tier 2; 30–59 -> Tier 3; < 30 -> Tier 4.
5) Attach classification to incident and follow the tiered remediation workflow below.

Context: production customers observed cases where long lived streaming sessions (tool calls + structured output) were left in indeterminate states after a client network disconnect or a client-initiated Cancel. Motivation: we need a predictable server-side safety net that bounds resource residency time, ensures tool-call idempotency when retries/resume occur, and provides a clear fallback path (trimmed response + final event) that OpenAI-compatible clients can rely on. This PR implements a server-side streaming timebox (configurable per-route) that gracefully converts oversized/inflight streams into a final 'timeboxed' terminal event, augments client-cancel handling to be idempotent across reconnect/resume windows, and plumbs a compact resume token that includes tool-call idempotency metadata. Summary of changes: 1) stream manager: add configurable timebox_ms and a deterministic finalization path that emits a structured terminal event ("__redwood_timeboxed__") with a compact summary; 2) openai adapter: interpret Cancel events as idempotent markers tied to resume tokens; retries within the resume window will deduplicate tool calls using a request-level id; 3) tooling: map function-call invocations to idempotency keys and persist minimal call metadata to the stream checkpoint to support safe resume; 4) API: extend the OpenAI-compat streaming spec with two optional fields in the final event (timeboxed=true, resume_hint) without breaking existing clients; 5) tests & docs: integration tests for flaky network simulated disconnects and release notes for the behavior and recommended operational knobs. Rollout plan: feature guarded behind a runtime flag and route-level config. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is unchanged unless a route opts-in. - request_id: short id (monotonic in manifest)

- sampling_config: temperature/top_k/top_p/typical_p/seed (if used)
- pre_hooks: list of transformations (name@version + diff/checksum) applied by client or proxy
- post_hooks: list of response transformations (e.g., de-identification, markup)
- expected_response_signature: optional small fingerprint of the original response to enable quick divergence checks

While the provided excerpts do not explicitly identify the GCP team as the source, Anika Desai recommended handling subscription entitlement delays by using a UX pattern that avoids "scary" error messages like "you are not entitled," instead using messaging such as "we’re still syncing your subscription, retry in a few minutes" and including a refresh button (dsid_6c4c1c875e704f09b4d791d64d7bc7e5.md). To bridge the gap between purchase and availability, recommended mechanisms include performing a sync every 5 minutes, using an on-demand process for onboarding, and implementing a manual fallback for support to force a sync (dsid_6c4c1c875e704f09b4d791d64d7bc7e5.md, dsid_3c9fe2220c204f13b878bd7d3a168f91.md, dsid_3c9mufe2220c204f13b878bd7d3a168f91.md).

*   The UX should include a "last checked at" timestamp to reassure the user that a process is active (dsid_6c4c1c875e704f09b4d791d64d7bc7e5.md).
*   Anika Desai recommends using the phrase "a few minutes" rather than specific durations like "2 minutes" or "10 minutes" to avoid over-promising (dsid_6c4c1c875 e704f09b4d791d64d7bc7e5.md).
*   The backend/architectural components should utilize an entitlement verification endpoint and a sync job to manage the process (dsid_6c4c1c875e704f09b4d791d64d7bc7e5.md).
*   The integration strategy should use the `consumerId` and entitlement name/resource received during subscription as the source of truth for determining subscription status and mapping metering events (dsid_6c4c1c875e704f09b4d791d64d7bc7e5.md).
*   For a console-based claim flow, the process should be validated by retrieving the entitlement status from the backend (dsid_6c4nt1c875e704f09b4d791d64d7bc7e5.md).
*   A manual fallback exists where support can verify a subscription ID and force a sync if needed (dsid_3c9mufe2220c204f13b878bd7d3a168f91.md).

- Trigger signal: normalized boolean or scalar indicating regional impairment or risk. - Decision: computed outcome (no-op, failover, partial shift, rollback, hold). - Action: executable change (policy flip, weight adjustment, circuit breaker mode) emitted by controller. Inputs / data model assumptions
- Policy engine receives inputs as a single evaluation payload, including:
  - route_id (e.g., hosted.chat.completions, dedicated.pool.<pool_id>)
  - tenant_id (optional for shared Hosted; required for Dedicated)
  - tenant_tier (free/pro/enterprise/dedicated)
  - current_routing_state (primary region, weights, last_flip_at)
  - signals (per region, per signal type):
    - reachability: ok|degraded|down + confidence + last_updated
    - errors_5xx_burn: burn_rate + window + confidence
    - tail_latency_burn: burn_rate + p95/p99 deltas + confidence
    - capacity_headroom: percent + “hard gate” boolean
    - control_plane_health (optional): ok|degraded|down
  - evaluation_time (UTC epoch + monotonic sequence)
  - constraints (policy-level + tenant-level): max_flips_per_hour, min_hold_down_seconds, require_approval, blast_radius_limit

Determinism requirements (core)
1) Stable ordering
- Evaluation must not depend on map iteration order. - Rule matching must define explicit ordering: by priority, then by tie-breakers. 2) Stable time semantics
- All windowed signals must be anchored to evaluation_time and include:
  - effective_start, effective_end, and a “freshness” timestamp. - Engine must treat stale signals consistently:
  - If authoritative signals are stale beyond threshold, decision = HOLD (do not fail over) unless reachability is explicitly DOWN with high confidence. 3) Single decision per evaluation
- For a given (route_id, tenant_id, evaluation_time), engine emits exactly one decision object, even if multiple actions are possible. - Multi-step actions (e.g., drain -> shift weights -> finalize) must be represented as a sequence recommendation but still within a single decision record.

If confidence < 50, do not auto-upgrade beyond Tier 3; route to on-call for manual triage and re-run enrichment after 5 minutes.
5) Combined score maps to Tier (v2 thresholds): Score >= 85 -> Tier 1; 70–84 -> Tier 2; 35–69 -> Tier 3; < 35 -> Tier 4.
6) Attach classification + confidence to incident and follow the tiered remediation workflow below.

C) Signal hierarchy evaluation (ADR-042)
Priority order (proposed canonical order for v1):
1) Reachability DOWN (authoritative) => FAILOVER (unless no healthy fallback)
2) Errors (5xx) fast burn (high severity) => FAILOVER or PARTIAL_SHIFT depending on blast radius and capacity
3) Tail latency burn (p99/p95) => PARTIAL_SHIFT first; escalate to FAILOVER if corroborated and sustained
4) Capacity exhaustion / hard gate => HOLD + load shed (controller action), avoid shifting into constrained region
5) Control plane degradation => HOLD (do not flip rapidly; prevent oscillation)

Notes:
- “No healthy fallback” means every eligible fallback region fails capacity_hard_gate OR reachability is down OR stale beyond threshold. - If no healthy fallback, decision should be HOLD and include “degrade_allowed=true” hint (controller can activate load shedding / retry-after). The provided draft specification does not explicitly define a single, numbered hierarchy or priority order for evaluating all failure signals; however, it establishes specific rules for signal priority and decision-making where "Reachability DOWN" is considered authoritative and given priority as a trigger for FAILOVER (dsid_184be937d34a412ab5e61366d54d8ed6.md).

*   In the signal hierarchy evaluation (ADR-042), "Reachability DOWN" is prioritized as an authoritative trigger for a FAILOVER decision (dsid_184be937d34a412ab5e61366d54d8ed6.md).
*   High severity triggers include 5xx error fast burns, which can result in either a FAILOVER or a PARTIAL_SHIFT depending on the capacity and the blast radius (dsid_184be937d34a412ab5e61366d54d8ed6.md).
*   Tail latency burn (p99/p95) is used to trigger a PARTIAL_SHIFT first, which may escalate to a FAILOVER if the signal is sustained and corroborated (dsid_184be937d34a412ab5e61366d54d8ed6.md).
*   Capacity exhaustion or a "hard gate" acts as a signal that can trigger a HOLD decision and load shedding to prevent shifting traffic into a region that is already constrained (dsid_184be937d34a412ab5e61366d54d8ed6.md).
*   Control plane degradation is a signal that can lead to a HOLD decision to prevent rapid oscillation (dsid_184be937d34a412ab5e61366d54d8ed6.md).
*   If authoritative signals are stale beyond a specific threshold, the engine's decision is set to HOLD (preventing failover) unless reachability is explicitly DOWN with high confidence (dsid_184be937d34a412ab5e61366d54d8ed6.md).
*   For production scopes, a requirement is being introduced to mandate at least one corroborating signal for reachability-based failover, such as 5xx burn, control-plane health, or sustained probe failure above a threshold (dsid_d844cc30147b49c69ea5275b4993b571.md).
*   The engine's core determinism requirements state that rule matching must define an explicit ordering "by priority, then by tie-breakers" (dsid_184be937d34a412ab5e61366d54d8ed6.md).
*   There is a conflict regarding the primary gate for decisions: dsid_7b2f4b37dfb642e19d78c5f9d2c43f16#0 states the system has standardized on p95 and error-rate and that p99 is no longer the primary gate, whereas dsid_184be937d34a412ab5e61366d54d8ed6.md includes p99 as part of the tail_latency_burn signal (p95/p99 deltas) used for evaluation.

Inputs / data model assumptions
- Policy engine receives inputs as a single evaluation payload, including:

Determinism requirements (core)
1) Stable ordering
- Evaluation must not depend on map iteration order. - Rule matching must define explicit ordering: by priority, then by tie-breakers. 2) Stable time semantics
- All windowed signals must be anchored to evaluation_time and include:
  - effective_start, effective_end, and a “freshness” timestamp. - Engine must treat stale signals consistently:
  - If authoritative signals are stale beyond threshold, decision = HOLD (do not fail over) unless reachability is explicitly DOWN with high confidence. 3) Single decision per evaluation
- For a given (route_id, tenant_id, evaluation_time), engine emits exactly one decision object, even if multiple actions are possible. - Multi-step actions (e.g., drain -> shift weights -> finalize) must be represented as a sequence recommendation but still within a single decision record.

C) Signal hierarchy evaluation (ADR-042)
Priority order (proposed canonical order for v1):
1) Reachability DOWN (authoritative) => FAILOVER (unless no healthy fallback)
2) Errors (5xx) fast burn (high severity) => FAILOVER or PARTIAL_SHIFT depending on blast radius and capacity
3) Tail latency burn (p99/p95) => PARTIAL_SHIFT first; escalate to FAILOVER if corroborated and sustained
4) Capacity exhaustion / hard gate => HOLD + load shed (controller action), avoid shifting into constrained region
5) Control plane degradation => HOLD (do not flip rapidly; prevent oscillation)

Notes:
- “No healthy fallback” means every eligible fallback region fails capacity_hard_gate OR reachability is down OR stale beyond threshold. - If no healthy fallback, decision should be HOLD and include “degrade_allowed=true” hint (controller can activate load shedding / retry-after). This document captures a reproducible experiment matrix for operator-driven fallback strategies and an associated cost-penalty catalog used to evaluate trade-offs between SLO preservation and unit economics across regional surges. ---------------

**Detection:**
- We detected the regression via:
  - SRE dashboards for failover signals (5xx burn + tail latency burn)
  - Routing policy flip counters (unexpected rate)
  - Support ping that a customer saw transient errors (correlated to test window)

**Response:**
- Disabled failover automation for the scoped policy (feature flag / controller disable). - Reduced gateway retry pressure using existing runtime/gateway knobs (temporary tuning) while traffic re-stabilized. - Confirmed eu-west capacity headroom and verified no persistent impairment. - Coordinated comms with Support: acknowledged planned test, explained transient errors, offered retry guidance. ## Root cause
The regression was caused by **policy oscillation** (flip/rollback) triggered by **noisy reachability signals**, combined with insufficient guardrails that allowed multiple routing policy changes in a short period. The oscillation produced a traffic pattern that:
1) **increased cross-region redirects**, and
2) **amplified retries** at the gateway/client level,
leading to transient overload and elevated error rates in the target region. Key technical drivers:
- **Reachability probes produced false positives** (brief, correlated failures) that were treated as authoritative without adequate corroboration. - **Hold-down and anti-flap timers were too permissive** for the observed signal volatility. - **Rollback semantics were correct per implementation**, but not aligned with our intended ADR-level behavior (we rolled back too quickly and re-triggered failover immediately).

- On-call and engineering coordination was fast; disabling automation stabilized the system quickly. - The team captured decision points and signal state changes in real time, enabling clear follow-up. ## What didn’t go well
- The automation acted faster than our operational ability to confirm whether the impairment was real. - We did not have a single “confidence score” view combining signal corroboration, dampening state, and decision rationale. - Support was notified quickly, but we did not proactively message a small set of known sensitive accounts before running the test (we relied on the planned-test guidance rather than a targeted heads-up). ## Where we got lucky
- eu-west had enough headroom that the overload was short-lived. - The oscillation stayed within a few minutes; a longer duration could have caused a larger SLO burn and broader customer impact. ## Immediate remediation (completed during/after the event)
- Disabled automation for the scoped policy upon observing oscillation. - Manual stabilization of routing preference and verification of regional health. - Support response guidance provided for inbound tickets about transient errors. ## Corrective and preventive actions (CPAs)
> This section is the contract: what we will change so a controlled test does not regress customer experience again. ### A. Trigger signal pipeline hardening
1) **Corroboration requirements**
   - Require at least one corroborating signal for reachability-based failover in production scopes (e.g., 5xx burn OR control-plane health OR sustained probe failure above threshold). - Owner: **Ravi Menon** (Routing policy)
   - Target: **2026-02-14**

2) **Dampening + hold-down tuning**
   - Increase minimum sustain time for reachability impairment and increase recovery hold-down. - Add jitter/TTL protections on health reads to avoid stampedes.

Overview
========

This document captures a reproducible experiment matrix for operator-driven fallback strategies and an associated cost-penalty catalog used to evaluate trade-offs between SLO preservation and unit economics across regional surges. It is intended for platform operators, SREs, and product engineers running controlled degradation experiments or designing automatic fallback policies. Why this exists
---------------
- Fallbacks are a major lever for preserving SLOs during capacity scarcity or model regressions, but they have measurable cost and quality impacts. - Operators need a concise experiment plan with metrics, dashboard queries, and a cost penalty model to compare candidate strategies. - This doc standardizes experiment telemetry, rollout/rollback steps, and decision criteria for productionizing fallbacks. Goals and scope
---------------
- Goal: Provide a repeatable experiment matrix that yields quantitative comparisons of: latency SLO retention, token-cost delta, quality regressions (evaluations), and operator intervention effort. - Scope: Multiregion inference surface (hosted + dedicated), model variant fallbacks (quantized, smaller model families), and routing degradations (regional drain, tenant throttling). - Out of scope: Model training/data pipelines, legal/customer contract negotiation. Definitions and abbreviations
---------------------------
- Fallback variant: Any alternative response path (e.g., model C => model B, or cached response) used when the primary path is unavailable or overloaded. - Cost penalty: Unit cost increase or revenue impact metric associated with using a fallback (e.g., tokens * $/token diff, or additional infra cost). - SLO preservation: Fraction of requests meeting 95th percentile latency target and error-rate SLO.

- Dashboard set used:
  - Failover signals overview
  - Route-level error/latency panels for allowlisted traffic
  - Region health (reachability + 5xx burn + latency burn)

## Recommendations for Game Day #2
- Tighten blast radius further: single route + single model family for first 15 minutes, then expand. - Require “per-pool headroom green” before shifting any Dedicated traffic. - Pre-announce internal-only status page entry to exercise comms workflow without confusing customers. - Ensure dashboard annotations are present and verified in a pre-flight checklist. ## Appendix: test configuration (high level)
- Allowlist: limited set of tenants tagged `tier=internal` and `tier=pilot`. - Controller: execute mode requires manual approval; max flips per hour enforced. - DNS/Anycast: no global DNS TTL changes executed during this test (routing policy only). ---

This PRD defines a production-ready evaluation harness for Optimize that: (1) uses cohort-driven and sentinel prompt sampling; (2) gates A/B rollouts with statistical and business thresholds; and (3) implements a graded rollback/failover policy that escalates from automated throttles to full traffic rollback. The goal is to reduce undetected regressions while keeping rollout velocity high for model and configuration updates. We have recurring incidents where model/config rollouts pass coarse checks but produce regression in specific customer cohorts or long-tail prompts. Current canaries are per-model and global; they miss cohort-specific quality regressions and provide coarse binary pass/fail decisions. Optimize needs a more granular, actionable evaluation contract that ties observable signals to deterministic remediation steps and human-in-the-loop triage when necessary.

- Secondary signal: Grafana dashboard showed many “regression detected” annotations without corresponding customer latency change. ## Timeline (UTC)
- **2026-02-12 16:05** – Expanded canary coverage from 3 → 8 models in us-east; enabled paging rule for “top models”. - **16:12** – First warning alerts fire for 3 models (p95 latency regression > threshold). Incident-bot starts threads. - **16:16** – Paging alerts begin for a top model; on-call acknowledges. - **16:18** – Additional paging alerts fire for multiple models; dedupe fails and creates multiple parallel threads. - **16:23** – Runtime on-call compares canary runtime-only latency vs customer e2e; no matching regression observed. - **16:28** – Telemetry team notices time series fragmentation: unexpected label combinations, very low samples per series. - **16:34** – SRE disables paging rules (keeps warnings) and increases dampening window. - **16:41** – Baseline store reads show frequent “baseline not found” with fallback to default thresholds. - **16:46** – Canary config rolled back to previous 3-model set; alert volume drops. - **17:02** – Incident declared resolved; follow-up investigation assigned. ## What happened (symptoms)
The canary’s regression evaluator compared observed p95 latency/tokens-sec against per-model baselines. After model expansion:
- Many evaluations used **fallback baseline values** because the baseline lookup key did not match (baseline existed under a different dimension set). - Metric series were fragmented by high-cardinality labels; the regression evaluator saw many “small-N” series and oscillated between “enough samples” and “not enough samples” depending on which series was queried. - Alert rules did not consistently enforce **minimum sample size across the same grouping** used by the evaluator, which allowed small, noisy slices to trip thresholds. - incident-bot dedupe keys lacked stable identifiers for (model, version, region, sku, runtime_build), so the same underlying symptom created repeated threads/pages.

It is intended to: align SRE, Product, and Customer Success during SLO degradations; minimize time-to-customer-remediation; and create consistent inputs for post-incident reviews and error-budget decisions.

Audience
- On-call SREs
- SRE leads and managers
- Incident commanders (ICs)
- Customer Success (CS) and Support for high-impact incidents

Principles
1) Tie every SLO alert to an explicit customer-impact tier (1–4).
2) Automate low-friction routing and remediation for common degradations.
3) Escalate proactively for any Tier 1/2 customer impact.
4) Preserve evidence for postmortems and error-budget reconciliations.

Definitions
- SLO: Service Level Objective (e.g., request_latency_p95 <= 200ms).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO target over the defined rolling window.
- Customer-impact tier: a 1–4 classification used to route and prioritize incident response.

Customer-impact tiers (quick guide)
| Tier | User-visible symptoms | Business effect | Escalation urgency | Owner to notify |
|------|----------------------|-----------------|-------------------|----------------|
| 1 | Widespread request failures or complete service outage across regions | Severe revenue/customer retention impact | Immediate (page) | SRE lead + Product PM + CS Director |
| 2 | Large subset of customers impacted (major tenants) or major feature down | Significant business disruption for key customers | High (page + slack) | SRE oncall + Product owner + CS manager |
| 3 | Localized errors, degraded latency for non-critical endpoints | Minor customer annoyance, limited support tickets | Medium (slack alert) | On-call SRE + Feature owner |
| 4 | Minor latency increase or transient errors with no customer tickets | No immediate business impact | Low (ticket) | On-call SRE |

Classification algorithm (operational)
1) Alert receives telemetry: detector alerts on SLI breach or error-budget burn (alerting config).
2) Metrics enrichment: pull impact signals (affected tenant count, region distribution, top N tenants by RPS, open support tickets matching pattern).
3) Heuristics engine evaluates the following scores (0–100): failure-scope, severity, customer-exposure.
4) Combined score maps to Tier: Score >= 80 -> Tier 1; 60–79 -> Tier 2; 30–59 -> Tier 3; < 30 -> Tier 4.
5) Attach classification to incident and follow the tiered remediation workflow below.

Tier 3 (Operational handling)

- Apply mitigations from the runbook: restart worker pool, clear KV cache, or disabled newly-deployed feature flag.

Tier 4 (Monitoring)
- Monitor metrics and let automated remediation run. If unresolved after SLA window (6 hours), escalate to Tier 3.

Purpose: quick, scannable personal notes for running the shiproom and weekly readiness sync. Organized as prep items, live-run cues, and follow-up actions. Not a polished playbook — my sticky running list + prompts to escalate. DAY-BEFORE / 24-48H CHECKS (quick hits)
- Validate Dedicated pool health dashboard (console > Dedicated > Pool-5). Look for 90th pct latency spike > 20% vs baseline. If spike: page SRE and tag 'pool-5'. - Confirm model pin assignments for weekend rollouts: model = rwx-v2-quant, pinned to image-2026-02-28. Cross-check with model-catalog ticket. - Ensure canary capacity reserved: 3 instances w/ low-priority burst. If not reserved, open ticket to infra (email infra-runbooks). - Verify last smoke-run results (smoke/last-run.json) — critical checks: health endpoints, prefix caching, stream stability. Mark any failing check with TODO. MEETING AGENDA (for my 10–15 min run)
1) Quick status (30s each): Hosted API, Dedicated, Private — 3 bullet lines max. 2) Go/No-Go candidate items (3) — call out owner for decision. 3) High-risk regressions & mitigations (A/B, rollbacks, fallback). 4) Open action items from last week (owners + ETA). 5) Escalations and customer-impacting items. GO/NO-GO CHECKLIST (my shorthand)
- Safety: latest canary passed golden prompt set? [yes/no] — if no -> NO-GO and block rollout. Owner: Priya. - Latency: 95th <= SLO (hosted) and Dedicated 90th within committed window? [ok/warn/fail] Owner: Jordan. - Throughput: capacity test at target qps for model variant (rwx-v2-quant) >= 90% predicted. Owner: Marco (perf eng). - Telemetry: traces + logs flowing to observability (no gaps > 5 min). Owner: Observability on-call. - Rollback plan: image rollback verified in staging (time-to-recover < 10m). Owner: me (Aisha) — pre-check: rehearse command set. LIVE-RUN CUES (during shiproom)
- If latency alert fires: call out metric, ask SRE to confirm impact (hosted vs dedicated). If impact is hosted only -> consider global throttles, otherwise trigger capacity burst.

- A4: Aisha (me) — rehearse rollback commands in staging and record exact steps in private playbook (due 2026-03-02). - A5: Eng-sre on-call — add trace tag for canary requests to make debugging faster (due 2026-03-03). NOTES-TO-SELF / RUN-TIME SNIPPETS
- Keep the Launch Channel pinned and set ephemeral notifications: only @here for major go/no-go decisions. - One-sentence status template for quick updates: "Area — short-state (ok/warn/fail) — top-1 mitigation if warn/fail". Use this when I call status. - If we need to delay: propose a 1-hour cool-down + redo canary after fixes. ESCALATION CONTACTS (quick)

**Customer content (MUST remain within pinned region(s))**
- Prompt / messages / input text (including system prompts provided by customer)
- Tool/function call arguments provided by customer
- Uploaded documents or retrieved passages (RAG payloads) provided by customer
- Model outputs (including partial streaming tokens)
- Embeddings input text and embeddings vectors derived from customer text
- Rerank inputs (candidate passages) and rerank outputs derived from those passages
- Fine-tuning / adapter payloads if routed through Hosted API pathways (not in scope for v1 feature, but classification applies)
- Any debug payloads that include raw request/response bodies
- Any derived artifacts that can reconstruct content (e.g., token logs, decoded segments, sampled prompt fragments)

**Not customer content (may be processed outside pinned region(s) under constraints below)**
- Non-content operational metadata that does not include request/response bodies and cannot reasonably be used to reconstruct them (see “Allowed cross-region metadata”). Notes:
- Whether content includes PII is not determinative; **all prompts/outputs are treated as sensitive content**. - “Derived” includes transformations (tokenization, embedding vectors, compression) if they are computed from customer text/output. ### 2) Enforcement boundary: “Where residency applies”
For pinned orgs/projects/API keys, **all handling of customer content** must remain in allowed region(s) for:
- **Request routing** and execution (including retries and fallbacks)
- **Background work** that uses the request payload or output (e.g., async logging of bodies, eval capture, replay queues)
- **Persistence and caching** of any form of request/response content
- **Observability signals** that contain content (logs/traces/debug captures)

Residency enforcement is evaluated at request time by the gateway/routing policy engine and must be **deterministic** (same policy + same request context → same allow/block outcome).

- Deterministic intent: include all inputs that can affect output (tokenizer, seed, model artifact id, runtime config, injected policies). - Portable: JSON-compatible, human-readable, and easy to attach to support tickets or GitHub issues. - Privacy-aware: fields that may contain PII must be flagged and optionally replaced with redaction pointers. Top-level fields (v1):
- manifest_id: short id (UUID recommended)
- created_by: name/email of the authoring agent (person, system)
- created_at: ISO date
- source_context: freeform string describing the scenario (UI flow, API route)
- requests: ordered list of request descriptors (see below)
- environment: runtime/environment snapshot (hardware/host tags, region, container image)
- model_artifact: model id + exact artifact checksum (sha256) + quantization profile id
- tokenizer: tokenizer version id + checksum + tokenizer config (if nonstandard)
- runtime_flags: map-like list of runtime knobs that influence execution (e.g., use_kv_cache=false)
- deterministic_seeds: list of PRNG seeds used for sampling or other non-deterministic logic
- telemetry_refs: pointers to associated logs, traces, and metric snapshots
- privacy_policy: small token describing redaction level (none, partial, strict)
- signature: optional signed blob for integrity verification (OIDC/JWKS compatible)

Request descriptor (ordered list element):
- request_id: short id (monotonic in manifest)
- timestamp: ISO timestamp of original request
- api_route: e.g., \"/v1/generate\" or \"/v1/chat/completions\"
- client_sdk: client library and version (if applicable)
- raw_payload_ref: pointer to stored payload (S3/GCS/secure-store) OR inline (redacted) string
- input_checksums: list of checksum objects (tokenization checksum, raw text checksum)
- sampling_config: temperature/top_k/top_p/typical_p/seed (if used)
- pre_hooks: list of transformations (name@version + diff/checksum) applied by client or proxy
- post_hooks: list of response transformations (e.g., de-identification, markup)
- expected_response_signature: optional small fingerprint of the original response to enable quick divergence checks
- fallback_policy_trace: if fallback occurred during original call (e.g., switched to smaller model), record decisions and timestamps

Environment (examples):
- host_os: ubuntu-22.04
- runtime_image: redwood/runtime-infer:2025-10-21
- gpu: a100-80gb (or cpu)
- region: us-west-2
- concurrency_profile: \"single-req\" | \"batched\"

Telemetry references:
These are URIs (or internal artifact ids) pointing to:
- structured trace (jaeger/span id)
- token-level metrics (latency per token)
- server logs (filtered range)
- resource utilization snapshot (GPU memory thread dump)

Privacy notes:
- raw_payload_ref should be used in combination with privacy_policy.

- capabilities: free-form tags that the eval mesh uses for routing (e.g., functioncall-validation, kv-cache-sensitive, quant-aware). - resource_hints: best-effort hints used by the orchestrator for capacity decisions. - outputs: relative file paths in the workdir that the plugin must produce. See "Outputs and artifact index" below. Sidecar plugin API (HTTP JSON v1)
- Endpoints and expected payloads:
  GET /healthz -> 200 {"status":"ok","version":"0.3.1"}
  POST /run -> 202 Accepts a RunSpec JSON, returns {"run_id":"uuid-v4","eta_seconds": int}
  POST /stop -> 200 Accepts {"run_id": ... , "signal": "graceful|force"}
  GET /status?run_id=<id> -> 200 {"run_id":..., "state":"running|completed|failed|stopped","progress":0.0}
  GET /artifact-index?run_id=<id> -> 200 returns the artifacts index JSON file

RunSpec JSON (stringified example)
{
  "run_id": "string (optional, auto-generated)",
  "slice_id": "string",
  "probe_manifest": "s3://.../slice-manifest.json",
  "seeds": [42, 7, 2026],
  "mode": "shadow|ci|local",
  "telemetry_level": "minimal|standard|verbose",
  "max_examples": 10000
}

Outputs and artifact index
- Required artifact outputs (placed in workdir/out/<run_id>/):
  - results.jsonl (newline-delimited JSON with standardized ResultEnvelope)
  - index.json (artifact index described below)
  - optional: html-report.zip, debug-traces.tar.gz

Artifact index JSON (index.json) - required fields (stringified example)
{
  "run_id": "uuid",
  "started_at": "ISO8601",
  "completed_at": "ISO8601",
  "results_file": "results.jsonl",
  "summary": "out/summary.json",
  "checksums": {"results.jsonl":"sha256:..."}, "telemetry_digest": "sha256:..."
}

ResultEnvelope (one per line in results.jsonl)
- Minimal fields: probe_id, input_hash, output_text, score (optional), metadata (map). - Example line:
{"probe_id":"anchor-003","input_hash":"sha256:...","output_text":"...","score":0.87,"metadata":{"seed":42,"latency_ms":123}}

The orchestration service communicates with: billing, routing, runtime control plane, monitoring, and the console.

- Components:
  - Migration Orchestrator (service): tracks state machine (estimate -> staging -> validate -> cutover -> reconcile -> archive).
  - Estimate Engine: runs simulation using historical token traces + model profiles to produce cost and SLO risk assessments.
  - Staging Proxy: routes a configurable percentage of production traffic to the new bundle variant for validation.
  - Billing Reconciler: coordinates dual-metering and credits.
  - SLO Validator: compares live metrics to baseline and flags pass/fail.

API contract examples:
- Estimate request (JSON)
```
POST /v1/migration/estimate
{
  "account_id": "acct_123",
  "lookback_days": 30,
  "models": ["redwood/gemini-13b", "open/guanaco-7b"],
  "target_bundle": "slo-standard"
}
```
- Example estimate response (abridged)
```
{
  "monthly_cost": "USD 12,400",
  "predicted_p95_delta": "+12%",
  "recommended_configuration": {"burst_capacity": "2000 rps", "quantization_profile": "q3"}
}
```

Migration phases and timeline (high level):
- Phase 0 (Prep, 0-2 weeks): product sign-off, legal T&Cs update, pricing modelling finalized, pilot cohort selected.
- Phase 1 (Pilot, 2-8 weeks): 5–10 reference customers, staging runs, end-to-end billing validation.
- Phase 2 (Scale rollout, 8-20 weeks): self-serve console enablement, sales enablement docs, automated reconciliations.
- Phase 3 (General availability, 20+ weeks): GA launch, public docs, migration incentives sunset.

Rollout steps (detailed numbered procedure):
1. Prepare account profile and collect 30-day telemetry snapshot.
2. Run Estimate Engine to generate cost + SLO risk.
3. Present migration plan to customer via Console and Sales.
4. If customer accepts, create staging proxy and route 1–5% traffic for 48 hours.
5. Run automated SLO validation. If pass, increment to 25% for 72 hours.
6.

Telemetry required for billing and performance tuning is accessible via console and APIs; customers can request deletion per data retention policies.

These are the current suggested gates (not absolute; document deviations in the report):
- Accept: p95 latency within 10% of baseline AND eval regression <= 3% AND hourly cost delta within budgeted threshold AND no sustained increase in 429/5xx. - Ramp: p95 within 15% and eval regression <= 6% with operator + product approval. - Abandon: p95 > 20% degradation OR eval regression > 10% OR customer harm signals spike (tickets/429s) OR unexpected safety regressions. Top-level fields (v1):
- manifest_id: short id (UUID recommended)
- created_by: name/email of the authoring agent (person, system)
- created_at: ISO date
- source_context: freeform string describing the scenario (UI flow, API route)
- requests: ordered list of request descriptors (see below)
- environment: runtime/environment snapshot (hardware/host tags, region, container image)
- model_artifact: model id + exact artifact checksum (sha256) + quantization profile id
- tokenizer: tokenizer version id + checksum + tokenizer config (if nonstandard)
- runtime_flags: map-like list of runtime knobs that influence execution (e.g., use_kv_cache=false)
- deterministic_seeds: list of PRNG seeds used for sampling or other non-deterministic logic
- telemetry_refs: pointers to associated logs, traces, and metric snapshots
- privacy_policy: small token describing redaction level (none, partial, strict)
- signature: optional signed blob for integrity verification (OIDC/JWKS compatible)

Request descriptor (ordered list element):
- request_id: short id (monotonic in manifest)
- timestamp: ISO timestamp of original request
- api_route: e.g., \"/v1/generate\" or \"/v1/chat/completions\"
- client_sdk: client library and version (if applicable)
- raw_payload_ref: pointer to stored payload (S3/GCS/secure-store) OR inline (redacted) string
- input_checksums: list of checksum objects (tokenization checksum, raw text checksum)
- sampling_config: temperature/top_k/top_p/typical_p/seed (if used)
- pre_hooks: list of transformations (name@version + diff/checksum) applied by client or proxy
- post_hooks: list of response transformations (e.g., de-identification, markup)
- expected_response_signature: optional small fingerprint of the original response to enable quick divergence checks
- fallback_policy_trace: if fallback occurred during original call (e.g., switched to smaller model), record decisions and timestamps

- Whether content includes PII is not determinative; **all prompts/outputs are treated as sensitive content**. - “Derived” includes transformations (tokenization, embedding vectors, compression) if they are computed from customer text/output. ### 2) Enforcement boundary: “Where residency applies”
For pinned orgs/projects/API keys, **all handling of customer content** must remain in allowed region(s) for:
- **Request routing** and execution (including retries and fallbacks)
- **Background work** that uses the request payload or output (e.g., async logging of bodies, eval capture, replay queues)
- **Persistence and caching** of any form of request/response content
- **Observability signals** that contain content (logs/traces/debug captures)

Residency enforcement is evaluated at request time by the gateway/routing policy engine and must be **deterministic** (same policy + same request context → same allow/block outcome).

Top-level fields (v1):
- manifest_id: short id (UUID recommended)
- created_by: name/email of the authoring agent (person, system)
- created_at: ISO date
- source_context: freeform string describing the scenario (UI flow, API route)
- requests: ordered list of request descriptors (see below)
- environment: runtime/environment snapshot (hardware/host tags, region, container image)
- model_artifact: model id + exact artifact checksum (sha256) + quantization profile id
- tokenizer: tokenizer version id + checksum + tokenizer config (if nonstandard)
- runtime_flags: map-like list of runtime knobs that influence execution (e.g., use_kv_cache=false)
- deterministic_seeds: list of PRNG seeds used for sampling or other non-deterministic logic
- telemetry_refs: pointers to associated logs, traces, and metric snapshots
- privacy_policy: small token describing redaction level (none, partial, strict)
- signature: optional signed blob for integrity verification (OIDC/JWKS compatible)

Request descriptor (ordered list element):
- request_id: short id (monotonic in manifest)
- timestamp: ISO timestamp of original request
- api_route: e.g., \"/v1/generate\" or \"/v1/chat/completions\"
- client_sdk: client library and version (if applicable)
- raw_payload_ref: pointer to stored payload (S3/GCS/secure-store) OR inline (redacted) string
- input_checksums: list of checksum objects (tokenization checksum, raw text checksum)
- sampling_config: temperature/top_k/top_p/typical_p/seed (if used)
- pre_hooks: list of transformations (name@version + diff/checksum) applied by client or proxy
- post_hooks: list of response transformations (e.g., de-identification, markup)
- expected_response_signature: optional small fingerprint of the original response to enable quick divergence checks

Existing alerts were per-route and per-quantile but lacked a compact way to group requests by 'stage footprint' and automatically route alerting weight to the stage(s) most likely responsible. What this PR does: 1) Adds a lightweight token_stage_cohort service that computes a deterministic cohort key per invocation based on stage-level metrics (token counts per stage, kv-cache hit pattern, decode-batch size) and stores short-lived cohort aggregates. 2) Introduces an alert route-matrix generator that consumes cohort rollups and emits alert bindings which bias escalation to the top-k stages for that route. 3) Adds a new dashboard focused on cohort drift, stage heatmaps, and per-cohort cost/latency breakdown to help oncall quickly validate root cause hypotheses. 4) Wires the generator into the existing alerting pipeline with a safe canary rollout and automatic quiet-window attenuation to avoid regressing noise. Compatibility and rollout: service defaults to read-only mode until flagged by a feature flag; alert generation starts cross-account in a low-sensitivity mode (only P90/P99) and is then ramped after 72h of monitoring. Testing: unit and integration tests added; ran a 48h synthetic replay against production-like traces (see test run in CI). It is intended to: align SRE, Product, and Customer Success during SLO degradations; minimize time-to-customer-remediation; and create consistent inputs for post-incident reviews and error-budget decisions.

Audience
- On-call SREs
- SRE leads and managers
- Incident commanders (ICs)
- Customer Success (CS) and Support for high-impact incidents

Principles
1) Tie every SLO alert to an explicit customer-impact tier (1–4).
2) Automate low-friction routing and remediation for common degradations.
3) Escalate proactively for any Tier 1/2 customer impact.
4) Preserve evidence for postmortems and error-budget reconciliations.

Definitions
- SLO: Service Level Objective (e.g., request_latency_p95 <= 200ms).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO target over the defined rolling window.
- Customer-impact tier: a 1–4 classification used to route and prioritize incident response.

Customer-impact tiers (quick guide)
| Tier | User-visible symptoms | Business effect | Escalation urgency | Owner to notify |
|------|----------------------|-----------------|-------------------|----------------|
| 1 | Widespread request failures or complete service outage across regions | Severe revenue/customer retention impact | Immediate (page) | SRE lead + Product PM + CS Director |
| 2 | Large subset of customers impacted (major tenants) or major feature down | Significant business disruption for key customers | High (page + slack) | SRE oncall + Product owner + CS manager |
| 3 | Localized errors, degraded latency for non-critical endpoints | Minor customer annoyance, limited support tickets | Medium (slack alert) | On-call SRE + Feature owner |
| 4 | Minor latency increase or transient errors with no customer tickets | No immediate business impact | Low (ticket) | On-call SRE |

SLO catalog excerpt (example mapping)
| SLO name | Metric | Target | Error-budget window | Default customer-impact tier |
|----------|--------|--------|--------------------|--------------------------|
| request_latency_p95_public | request_latency_p95{route=~"/v1/.*"} | <= 200ms | 30d | 2 |
| api_error_rate_5m | sum(rate(api_errors[5m])) / sum(rate(api_requests[5m])) | <= 0.5% | 7d | 1 |
| embedding_throughput_tail | embedding_infer_latency_p99 | < 1.2s | 14d | 3 |
| console_ui_availability | synthetic_check(console_login) | 99.5% monthly | 30d | 3 |

Classification algorithm (operational)
1) Alert receives telemetry: detector alerts on SLI breach or error-budget burn (alerting config).
2) Metrics enrichment: pull impact signals (affected tenant count, region distribution, top N tenants by RPS, open support tickets matching pattern).
3) Heuristics engine evaluates the following scores (0–100): failure-scope, severity, customer-exposure.
4) Combined score maps to Tier: Score >= 80 -> Tier 1; 60–79 -> Tier 2; 30–59 -> Tier 3; < 30 -> Tier 4.
5) Attach classification to incident and follow the tiered remediation workflow below.

- affected_tenant_ratio: percent of total tenant RPS impacted.

Top-level fields (v1):
- manifest_id: short id (UUID recommended)
- created_by: name/email of the authoring agent (person, system)
- created_at: ISO date
- source_context: freeform string describing the scenario (UI flow, API route)
- requests: ordered list of request descriptors (see below)
- environment: runtime/environment snapshot (hardware/host tags, region, container image)
- model_artifact: model id + exact artifact checksum (sha256) + quantization profile id
- tokenizer: tokenizer version id + checksum + tokenizer config (if nonstandard)
- runtime_flags: map-like list of runtime knobs that influence execution (e.g., use_kv_cache=false)
- deterministic_seeds: list of PRNG seeds used for sampling or other non-deterministic logic
- telemetry_refs: pointers to associated logs, traces, and metric snapshots
- privacy_policy: small token describing redaction level (none, partial, strict)
- signature: optional signed blob for integrity verification (OIDC/JWKS compatible)

Request descriptor (ordered list element):
- request_id: short id (monotonic in manifest)
- timestamp: ISO timestamp of original request
- api_route: e.g., \"/v1/generate\" or \"/v1/chat/completions\"
- client_sdk: client library and version (if applicable)
- raw_payload_ref: pointer to stored payload (S3/GCS/secure-store) OR inline (redacted) string
- input_checksums: list of checksum objects (tokenization checksum, raw text checksum)
- sampling_config: temperature/top_k/top_p/typical_p/seed (if used)
- pre_hooks: list of transformations (name@version + diff/checksum) applied by client or proxy
- post_hooks: list of response transformations (e.g., de-identification, markup)
- expected_response_signature: optional small fingerprint of the original response to enable quick divergence checks
- fallback_policy_trace: if fallback occurred during original call (e.g., switched to smaller model), record decisions and timestamps

Summary

This page documents a repeatable, instructor-led bootcamp to train platform operators and engineers to write high-quality runbooks that are telemetry-driven, testable, and maintainable. The curriculum is designed for new operators, service owners, and incident responders who will author or own runbooks for platform services (prefix cache, allocator, tenant-slicing, model-variant router). Audience

- Platform operators and SREs
- Service owners in eng-platform and eng-serving-runtime
- Oncall engineers who respond to latency/cost incidents

Learning objectives (measurable)

1. Produce a runbook that contains a clear escalation path, data-driven detection predicates, and an operator checklist. 2. Write two telemetry queries (one metric-based, one log-based) that reliably surface the condition the runbook describes. 3. Create a synthetic verification (unit) that validates the runbook’s detection predicates against a small replay dataset. 4. Implement a post-incident update cycle and link to the action in the runbook so it can be closed by the owner. Curriculum overview (3-day instructor-led)

Day 0 — Prework (self-paced)
- Read: "Runbook authoring and maintenance guidelines" (required). - Complete a short quiz on SLO definitions and common platform failure modes. - Setup: access to Grafana/Tempo, Kibana, and a sandbox tenant. Confirm permissions with infra-oncall. Day 1 — Foundations and detection
- Morning: Lecture (1.5 hr) — Runbook structure and the telemetry-first principle. - Sections: Summary, Impact, Detection (metric + log predicates), Immediate actions, Escalation, Rollback, Postmortem link. - Example services: kv-prefix-cache, dynamic-allocator, model-variant-router. - Lab (2.5 hr): Write detection predicates for a synthetic latency spike:
  1) Metric predicate: p95 latency > 300ms for 5m AND error rate > 1% for 2m. 2) Log predicate: queries that include "kv-cache:miss" and "eviction-reason=reshuffle" for >50 events in 10m. - Homework: Author a first draft runbook for a provided scenario.

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Dashboard panels - [x] Docs for oncall and runbook - [x] Feature-flagged rollout Plan for operators: deploy to staging -> enable feature flag -> monitor cohort drift and false-positive rate -> bump sensitivity -> full rollout. Heuristics inputs (examples)

Operational remediations by tier
Tier 1 (Immediate response)
- Page the SRE oncall and SRE lead (PagerDuty service: customer-impact).
- Open an incident in the incident-management system using template tag=CUSTOMER_IMPACT_TIER_1 (auto-created if classifier confidence >= 70).
- Run mitigation playbook: fallback-to-compatible-model-variant.
- If capacity-related: trigger immediate capacity burst policy (see CLI below).
- Notify CS and Product leadership within 10 minutes with templated Slack/Jira.

Tier 2 (High-priority)
- Page on-call (high urgency) and post to #incidents.
- Execute targeted throttles or tenant fair-share configuration.
- Begin canary rollback of recent model or config changes (if correlated).

Tier 3 (Operational handling)
- Create ticket and schedule on-call investigation within 30–60 minutes.
- Apply mitigations from the runbook: restart worker pool, clear KV cache, or disable newly-deployed feature flag.

Tier 4 (Monitoring)
- Monitor metrics and let automated remediation run. If unresolved after SLA window (4 hours), escalate to Tier 3.

The root cause was identified as the switch's 'proxy-arp' feature injecting "gratuitous" ARP replies for VPN client IPs, which occurs specifically when the AP's multicast queue exceeds a certain threshold. This caused the switch to return ARP replies for the same IP address using an incorrect MAC address (00:66:77:88:99:AA) that matches a spare management interface in rack 7 (dsid_59cb294da8964683bb165a3bb615df71.md).

*   The frequency of these issues increases when there is a short burst of multicast/mDNS traffic on the same AP's radio (dsid_59cb294da8964683bb165a3bb615df71.md).
*   Priya Shah (campus-net) reproduced these proxy-arp responses on edge-sw-7 when the AP multicast queue was greater than 70% and noted that firmware 1.2.3 on these switches has a known bridging bug (dsid_59cb294da8964683bb165a3bb615df71.md).
*   The resulting connectivity blackholes lasted 30-90s and affected approximately 8% of VPN sessions in the SF2 us-west site, manifesting as frequent VPN re-auth events and TCP reset spikes in internal services (dsid_59cb294da8964683bb165a3bb615df71.md).
*   A packet capture (pcap) confirmed the presence of ARP replies for the same IP (10.23.8.45) using two different source MACs within a 120ms window (dsid_59cb294da8964683bb165a3bb615df71.md).
*   There is a conflict in dsid_59cb294da8964683bb165a3bb615df71.md regarding the specific configuration issue: one part of the file (chunk_a) presents a hypothesis that the edge switch's proxy-arp is configured for a legacy NAT path and is responding to ARP for VPN-assigned addresses from an overlapping DHCP pool, while another part (chunk_b) identifies the cause as the 'proxy-arp' feature injecting replies specifically when the AP's multicast queue exceeds a threshold.
*   There is a conflict between dsid_59cb294da8964683bb165a3bb615df71#1 and dsid_e728a420a02a4ddcb125e6adb09d211e#1 regarding the root cause: the former identifies a misconfigured VXLAN/bridge on edge-sw-7 causing ARP proxy-arp replies during multicast bursts, while the latter identifies a different VPN-related authentication failure caused by an office bridge (Ubiquiti UBB-Edge v2) set to 'Gateway (NAT)' mode instead of 'Bridge' mode (dsid_59cb294da8964683bb165a3bb615df71.md; dsid_e728a420a02a4ddcb125e6adb09d211e).

Scope:
Applies to: Redwood-hosted ingress proxies and customer-managed sidecar proxies that perform request fanout to model serving pools (Hosted, Dedicated, Private). Not intended for client SDK bugs or pure model runtime failures (see separate model runtime runbooks).

Background and root-cause patterns observed:
We have observed several distinct contributing factors across incidents:

1) Ephemeral port churn + NAT table exhaustion on stateful edge proxies, causing new connections to fail with RST or be reset after TLS handshake.
2) Imbalanced keepalive and health-check interactions where load balancer probes evict live backend sessions during short surges.
3) TLS session cache miss patterns combined with aggressively small client TLS timeouts that increase backend CPU and cause transient overload.
4) Fanout amplification when a single client request fans out to multiple model variants and an upstream slow backend causes head-of-line timeouts.

Symptoms (how customers and SREs will notice this):
- Short, periodic spikes of 502/503/504 errors concentrated to specific ingress proxies (not whole region).
- Error rates correlated to increase in ephemeral port allocation (netstat / ss shows many TIME_WAIT).
- Backend model nodes show normal CPU but elevated accept queue length or connection backlog.
- Trace IDs show upstream TLS handshake succeeded but the first application read returns EOF or ECONNRESET.
- Synthetic journey checks show success for HEAD requests but POST/generation endpoints intermittently fail.

Immediate mitigation runbook (for oncall/customer success):
Priority: restore traffic to customers with minimal impact; preserve telemetry for root-cause analysis.

1) Triage and scope (5–10 minutes)
   - Identify impacted tenants via the error-metrics dashboard (Route: Ingress > proxy-errors by route).
   - Narrow to proxy host(s) using service host labels and trace sampling: search traces for error=502 and group by proxy_hostname.
   - If >50% of requests to a given proxy host are failing, treat as full node degradation.

2) Short-term mitigations (10–30 minutes)
   a) Drain and replace affected proxy instance(s):
      - Mark the proxy node as draining in the autoscaler (CLI):
        kubectl annotate node <proxy-pod> redwood.run/drain=true --overwrite
      - Wait for healthy hosts to absorb connections (~30s–2m).
   b) Enable aggressive TCP keepalive tuning for edge proxies (hotfix):
      - For Linux hosts, set: sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1; sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_limit=50; sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog=2048
   c) Temporary fanout throttling: switch the fanout policy to sequential or limit to N variants for the affected tenant: update route override in routing-config: 
      - routing-cli set-fanout --route <route> --mode sequential --max-variants 2
   d) If TLS session cache is disabled on the proxy, re-enable with a conservative size (e.g., 10k entries) to reduce handshake load.

3) Customer communication (parallel)
   - Notify affected customers with current scope and ETA: use template 'ingress-interruption-brief' and include mitigations applied and expected next update in 30 minutes.

4) Preserve for RCA (ongoing)
   - Increase trace sampling rate to 25% for the impacted route for the next 2 hours.
   - Capture tcpdump (90s) on affected proxy: sudo tcpdump -w /tmp/proxy-eth0-<ts>.pcap host <client-ip> and upload to incident artifact storage.

Diagnostic steps (deeper root cause analysis):
1) Metrics to query (example PromQL):
   - ingress_proxy_connection_errors_total{code=~"5.."}
   - node_tcp_time_wait_total{instance=~"<host>"}
   - proxy_tls_handshake_duration_seconds_bucket
   - proxy_accept_queue_length{instance=~"<host>"}

2) Log patterns to search (example):
   - "accept: too many open files" in proxy logs
   - "EOF while reading from socket" or "unexpected EOF" in backend service logs
   - Repeated TLS session cache misses (log key: tls_cache_miss=true)

3) Trace analysis approach:
   - Correlate client-side span timestamps to server accept/dispatch spans.

- Trigger signal: normalized boolean or scalar indicating regional impairment or risk. - Decision: computed outcome (no-op, failover, partial shift, rollback, hold). - Action: executable change (policy flip, weight adjustment, circuit breaker mode) emitted by controller. Inputs / data model assumptions
- Policy engine receives inputs as a single evaluation payload, including:
  - route_id (e.g., hosted.chat.completions, dedicated.pool.<pool_id>)
  - tenant_id (optional for shared Hosted; required for Dedicated)
  - tenant_tier (free/pro/enterprise/dedicated)
  - current_routing_state (primary region, weights, last_flip_at)
  - signals (per region, per signal type):
    - reachability: ok|degraded|down + confidence + last_updated
    - errors_5xx_burn: burn_rate + window + confidence
    - tail_latency_burn: burn_rate + p95/p99 deltas + confidence
    - capacity_headroom: percent + “hard gate” boolean
    - control_plane_health (optional): ok|degraded|down
  - evaluation_time (UTC epoch + monotonic sequence)
  - constraints (policy-level + tenant-level): max_flips_per_hour, min_hold_down_seconds, require_approval, blast_radius_limit

Determinism requirements (core)
1) Stable ordering
- Evaluation must not depend on map iteration order. - Rule matching must define explicit ordering: by priority, then by tie-breakers. 2) Stable time semantics
- All windowed signals must be anchored to evaluation_time and include:
  - effective_start, effective_end, and a “freshness” timestamp. - Engine must treat stale signals consistently:
  - If authoritative signals are stale beyond threshold, decision = HOLD (do not fail over) unless reachability is explicitly DOWN with high confidence. 3) Single decision per evaluation
- For a given (route_id, tenant_id, evaluation_time), engine emits exactly one decision object, even if multiple actions are possible. - Multi-step actions (e.g., drain -> shift weights -> finalize) must be represented as a sequence recommendation but still within a single decision record.

The recommended two-stage process for rotating signing credentials consists of Phase A: Preflight (no live swap) and Phase B: Cutover (the swap) (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md). To cut over safely, an atomic alias swap is performed (kms/gpu-image-signer -> key-vN), followed by the promotion of a canary image signed with the new key to verify health via latency and error metrics for 20 minutes (dsid_f1b208\_f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md). If something goes wrong during the cutover, the system should revert the alias to the previous version (key-v(N-1)) and mark the new key (key-vN) as "revocation-pending" for forensic review (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).

**Phase A: Preflight (no live swap)**
*   Provision a new KMS key version and create the alias `kms/gpu-image-signer -> key-vN` (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   Deploy CI adapters (`sign-image-action`) in a feature-flagged mode to perform 100% test-signings that do not alter the promotion ledger (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   Verify that attestation services accept `key-vN` signatures (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   Run shadow cross-account copies using an ephemeral role with the new signing metadata to confirm successful copies across all target regions (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   Monitor for 24 hours or 3 release windows to check for unexpected pull authentication regressions (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).

**Phase B: Cutover (the swap)**
*   Schedule a change window with a target SLO of less than a 30-minute blind window (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   Perform an atomic alias swap: `kms/gpu-image-signer -> key-vN` (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   Revoke short-lived CI credentials associated with `key-v(N-1)` after a 5-minute grace period and rotate ephemeral role sessions (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   Promote a canary image signed with `key-vN` and verify canary health for 20 minutes across error and latency metrics (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   Proceed to full fleet promotion if no triggers are fired; if triggers are fired, revert the alias to `key-v(N-1)` and mark `key-vN` as `revocation-pending` for forensic review (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).

**Rollback and Emergency Procedures**
*   If pull authentication failures are $\ge$ 3% across $\ge$ 2 regions, run: `./scripts/revoke-ci-ephemeral-sessions --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ci-ephemeral-publisher` (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   If an image signature mismatch is reported, quarantine the image tag by marking it as `blocked` in the promotion ledger (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   If problems persist for more than 10 minutes, revert the registry image tag on affected warm pools to the previous production tag using `terraform apply -var='image_tag=${PREV_TAG}'` (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   Recreate node groups by triggering a `warm-pool rolling-replace` job if nodes are stuck (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).

**Monitoring and Detection**
*   Detection triggers include a pager firing for pull authentication failures or mass `pod CrashLoopBackOff` when pulling production images (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   Verification of the rollback decision requires confirming the presence and percentage of pull authentication errors via cross-region registry metrics (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   Required telemetry dashboards must include registry pull success rates by region and account (using 1m and 5m windows), image signature verification failures by key-version, canary latency and error rate trends compared to the baseline, and a promotion job success/failure histogram by commit (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).

**Conflicts and Contradictions**
*   The question asks for "Stage 1" and "Stage 2," but dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md uses the terms "Phase A: Preflight" and "Phase B: Cutover," whereas dsid_db1c_f8 describes a migration process as "Phase 1 (Pilot)" and "Phase 2 (Scale rollout)" (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md vs dsid_db1c_f8).
*   Regarding the primary rollback mechanism for credentials: dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md states that if triggers fire during cutover, the action is to "revert the alias to key-v(N-1)," but another section of the same file describes an emergency rollback action of running a script to revoke CI ephemeral sessions if pull authentication failures reach $\ge$ 3% across $\ge$ 2 regions (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   Regarding persistent problem resolution: dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md describes the rollback of the credential/alias as "revert alias to key-v(N-1)," but a different section of the same file describes the action for "If problems persist >10m" as reverting the registry image tag via Terraform (dsid_f1b208f3637e4987aeab371242a5bea5.md).
*   Regarding the manifest signature format: dsid_834de01417d04878b4257f0f03ccbb88 describes the 'signature' as an 'optional signed blob for integrity verification' within the top-level fields of the manifest, whereas dsid_2f9c99fc8ec74495b4b08c49a6083ba8 states that cryptographic signing is supported via references (`integrity` + `integrity_ref`) rather than an embedded blob (dsid_834de01417d04878b4257f0f03ccbb88 vs dsid_2f9c99fc8ec74495b4b08c49a6083ba8).

Summary

Purpose
This document defines a safety-first pattern for: (1) rotating CI credentials used by GPU provisioning and image-promotion pipelines, and (2) promoting GPU runtime images (golden bundles) to production pools with provable checks and fast rollback paths. The kit bundles Terraform/IaC patterns, CI job templates, runtime verification checks, SLO-driven gating, and an operator runbook for emergency credential revocation. Why this matters
- Credential rotation without careful orchestration can leave running inference pools unable to pull images, causing degraded capacity and failed deployments. - Image promotion (CI -> staging -> prod) must be atomic and verifiable: a mismatched image in a GPU pool can produce model-regression incidents. - Past incidents show the majority of image-promotion outages occur during key rotation + cross-account image copy windows. This doc reduces blast radius. Scope
Applies to: all CI pipelines that build GPU runtime images, the Terraform modules that provision tenant GPU hosts and warm pools, and the image-signing/attestation services used by Redwood Inference. Owner and contacts
- Owner team: engineering (Infra Reliability)
- Primary oncall for rollout windows: infra-oncall@redwood.com
- Escalation: Diego Ramos (Lead - GPU Infra), Priya Shah (Security), Evan Liu (CI/CD)

Terminology
- Golden image: signed OCI image bundle used for production inference nodes. - Image promoter: CI job that signs, copies, and tags artifacts into the production registry. - Promotion window: the short period where an image transitions from staging to prod and cross-account copies may be in-flight. Safety principles (high level)
1) Always sign images with key versioning (KMS key alias + key-id). Verification must include key version metadata. 2) Use a promotion plan that stages in-region canaries before full fleet promotion. 3) Make credential rotation a two-phase operation: preflight (test) then swap (cutover) with automatic rollback on failure.
